w: Cincinnati's only James Beard honoree for chili (America's Classic, 2000) — a 24-hour parlor since 1940. Order the 5-way: spaghetti, cinnamon-clove chili, kidney beans, diced onion and a mountain of shredded cheddar; the cheese coneys are the sleeper order.

The defining Cincinnati-chili brand, founded 1949 by Greek immigrant Nicholas Lambrinides. The downtown parlor is the classic city stop for a cheese coney (mustard, chili, mound of cheddar) and the 4-way onion.
sources: 10Best readers' polls repeatedly rank Skyline atop Cincinnati chili — see USA Today 10Best Cincinnati chili

w: A neighborhood parlor run by three generations of the Sideris family since 1964, beloved as much for its award-winning gravy cheese fries as its 2-through-5-way chili and homemade coneys.

Skyline's cross-town rival, born 1965 in Mt. Washington as 'Hamburger Heaven' before the Daoud brothers' chili took over the menu. The original location is the spot for a Gold Star cheese coney and 4-way.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Star_Chili — founded 1965, Mt. Washington, Daoud brothers

w: A 1969 Blue Ash institution twice featured on Guy Fieri's 'Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives' — he called the 5-way something he'd eat every day. Add jalapenos for the house 6-way.
sources: wcpo.com/best-cincinnati-chili-restaurants — Top chili parlors in the Tri-State

w: A West Side family restaurant since 1962 with the Golden Fleece Lounge attached — Cincinnati chili 2-through-5-way, cheese coneys, Greek favorites and big all-day breakfasts.
Northern Kentucky's first chili parlor, founded 1929 by Nicholas Sarakatsannis and still slinging 3-, 4- and 5-ways and coneys into the small hours across the river in Newport.
A sassy pink diner (since 1941) famous for 'wispy thin' pancakes and crisp-griddled goetta — the German pork-and-oats loaf that is Cincinnati's own breakfast meat.
sources: Cincinnati breakfast institution — wcpo.com coverage; also Roadfood.com

w: An old-fashioned Findlay Market butcher, family-run since 1852, voted Cincinnati's Best Goetta and selling 400-500 lbs a week — the goetta many city diners (including Tucker's) buy to griddle. Grab a loaf plus the house mettwurst.
sources: Twice voted 'Best Goetta' by Cincinnati Magazine — cincinnatifoodtours.com/blog/cincinnati-goetta; local12.com Eckerlin coverage

w: Cincinnati's 'Ribs King' since 1951 — Ted Gregory's slow-cooked ribs lacquered in Matula Gregory's sweet tangy sauce. The original Montgomery Road room is the mothership (a downtown Boathouse followed in 1989).
A riverside East End smoke shack that turned into a Cincinnati favorite: hickory pulled pork, ribs, all-beef dogs and the cult jalapeno-cheddar grits. Cash-friendly, picnic-table casual.
sources: Frequent Cincinnati Magazine BBQ pick; cincinnatibites.com/reviews/elis-bbq/
Repeatedly cited among the city's best BBQ — citybeat.com food coverage

w: Cincinnati's standout Vietnamese kitchen, grown from a Findlay Market stall (2011) to a full Race Street room with a bar. 20-hour broth from Ohio Sakura Farms Wagyu, lemongrass grilled pork, sharp banh mi.
Began 2007 as a 120-lb cast-iron waffle iron in the back of a Findlay Market produce shop; now the caramelized-sugar Liege waffle and the waffle-and-fried-chicken are a Cincinnati brunch signature.
sources: Cincinnati Magazine dining coverage of Taste of Belgium's Findlay Market origin

w: French-pot ice cream, hand-packed 2.5-gallon batches since 1870, with giant chocolate chunks. Cincinnati Magazine named the black raspberry chip a flavor that 'defines' the city; the Hyde Park scoop shop is the classic stop.
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeter's — Cincinnati Magazine named black raspberry chip a defining city food (2004)
Cincinnati Magazine — black raspberry chip among foods that define Cincinnati

dish: French pot ice cream & opera creams
w: An Oakley Square parlor barely changed since 1913 — Portuguese marble, Tiffany lamps, hand-laid tile — where the Greek Aglamesis family still makes French-pot ice cream and hand-dipped chocolates.

O'Bryonville patisserie (since 1983) whose signature is the Opera Cream Torte — dark chocolate, white chocolate and vanilla opera cream, a distinctly Cincinnati confection — plus schnecken and whimsical iced cookies.
A hometown tradition since 1928, best known for the yellow-iced 'smiley' cookie (a Cincinnati billboard icon) and buttery schnecken. The Hyde Park shop is the flagship counter.
Family-run since 1960 and repeatedly called Cincinnati's gold-standard doughnut — hand-cut, hand-dipped, from glazed to maple-bacon. Loveland is the original shop (the OTR location has since closed).
sources: USA Today 10Best Readers' Choice — Holtman's ranked among best U.S. doughnut shops

w: A Covington Westside beer hall built on scratch-ground German sausages — Feuerwurst, currywurst, apple-honey wurst — with schnitzel, giant pretzels with beer cheese and 40+ German/craft taps.
The Cincinnati pizza icon: Buddy LaRosa opened here in 1954 using his Aunt Dena's Sicilian recipe (sweeter provolone-topped pies). The original Westwood parlor is the fan-favorite original.

Wood-fired pies from a restored 150-year-old Walnut Hills firehouse (Engine Co. #16) — a rotating menu of blistered-crust specialty pizzas backed by a deep local beer list. The city's best neighborhood wood-fired option.
